purpose: Bounded Census household-level care-to-work record preserving paid-care cost, inadequate-care exposure, adaptation choices, and open later household outcomes.

events.geography: United States; CPS ASEC 2025 household report about 2024 child-care conditions
events.denominator: About 30.4 million U.S. households reporting a child age 13 or younger; affected-care and paid-care results use their stated subgroups
events.method: Structured extraction from the official Census working-paper summary of CPS ASEC 2025 findings
events.missingness: The public layer does not retain household identifiers, provider identity or closure date, subsidy or leave eligibility, commute, informal-care hours, exact wage loss, child outcome, later wave, or household-level sequence among multiple adaptations
events.exposure: Households reported paid-care use, care costs, problems obtaining adequate care, or care-related work-time loss; 3.7% reported problems obtaining adequate care and those households reported an average 65.8 days of work time lost
events.alternatives_before_action: The reported adaptation menu includes paid care, unpaid or family care, paid or unpaid leave, fewer hours, quitting, non-search, and supervising children while working; the source does not identify which feasible alternatives each household had
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Paid-care households spent about $10,520 on average, equal to about 5.6% of household income; inadequate-care households reported substantial work-time loss, while lower-income households were more likely to stay out of the labor market
events.choice_or_response: Households used overlapping work and care adaptations including leave, cutting hours, quitting, being fired, not looking for work, or supervising children while working
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Households selected among constrained care and work arrangements; providers, employers, family networks, subsidies, and local supply shaped the available option set, but the public layer does not identify control for each household
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: The public record describes paid-care use and work adaptations but does not document a household-specific subsidy, provider remedy, employer response, or completed institutional intervention
events.immediate_outcome: Care need was converted into different combinations of payment, unpaid time, work-time loss, labor-force withdrawal, or work-plus-supervision
events.protected_outcome: Some households preserved a formal work connection through paid care, leave, reduced hours, or supervising while working; the source does not establish adequacy or child wellbeing
events.sacrificed_outcome: Households could sacrifice income, work hours, job search, career stability, rest, care quality, or unpaid family time; the public results do not assign each sacrifice to the same household
events.cost_risk_transfer: Care constraints can transfer cost from a visible payment into lost work, unpaid family labor, reduced job quality, or labor-market exit; the cross-sectional source does not identify the full household balance
events.later_outcome: Later care arrangement, work return, earnings, debt, health, child wellbeing, household security, trust, and exit are not followed
events.meaning_and_attribution: The source supports a material and work-constraint interpretation, but does not measure household meaning, blame, trust, or attribution to a provider, employer, or policy
events.public_or_collective_response: The published layer does not report household complaint, organizing, political action, or later policy response
events.counterexample: Low paid-care spending can coexist with high burden when a household cannot buy care and instead loses work time or leaves the labor market
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official Census working paper, https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2026/demo/sehsd-wp2026-08.html; reported household averages and adaptation categories are descriptive and not a causal estimate

arrows.to: paid care, unpaid support, or care-work disruption
arrows.evidence: The Census layer reports paid-care use, problems obtaining adequate care, and an adaptation menu
arrows.counterexample: Paid-care use is not proof of adequate care and low paid use is not proof of low need
arrows.remaining_gap: Household-level provider, family-support, subsidy, and disruption sequence

arrows.to: leave, reduced hours, quitting, non-search, or work-plus-supervision
arrows.evidence: The official summary reports these adaptation categories among households with child-care problems
arrows.counterexample: The categories may overlap and do not establish one household's ordered pathway or job causation
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-household adaptation order, employer response, and feasible alternatives

arrows.to: work-time loss and household cost transfer
arrows.evidence: Households reporting care problems reported an average 65.8 days of work time lost; paid-care households reported average spending of about $10,520
arrows.counterexample: Work-time loss is not the same as wage loss, permanent exit, or a causal estimate; cost averages are conditional on paid care
arrows.remaining_gap: Household-specific earnings, unpaid time, debt, job quality, and protected outcome

arrows.to: later care stability, child wellbeing, work return, security, or exit
arrows.evidence: The public Census layer is retrospective and cross-sectional and does not follow households into a later period
arrows.counterexample: A household can preserve formal employment while losing hours, rest, income, or care quality; later recovery cannot be inferred
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-household later care arrangement, work/earnings, child outcome, health, security, trust, and exit

boundary: This ledger closes a reported household care-to-work adaptation surface but does not establish causality, a same-household later outcome, provider adequacy, or child wellbeing.
storage_boundary: No CPS microdata or household identifiers are retained; only bounded official aggregate findings and explicit open downstream arrows are represented.
